analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run Medicare drug plan and lets Medicare negotiate drug prices directly.
analysis.headline: A bill to have Medicare negotiate drug prices drew 133 cosponsors, including one Republican, but never got a committee vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare's 2003 drug benefit (Part D) pays private insurance companies and pharmacy-benefit middlemen to buy prescriptions for seniors, and it bars the government from negotiating prices with drug makers. This bill would add a Medicare-run drug plan sold in every state, let the Secretary of Health and Human Services negotiate prices with pharmaceutical manufacturers directly, and cap the premium at $35 a month in 2006. It went to two committees and a subcommittee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, roughly the millions of seniors and disabled Americans enrolled in the new Part D drug benefit, who would get a lower-cost government-run plan option and the benefit of negotiated drug prices [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer at least one Medicare-operated prescription drug plan available nationwide, alongside the private Part D plans, so every beneficiary has a public option [S2][S3].

Directs the Secretary to negotiate directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers over the purchase price of covered Part D drugs and to encourage cheaper therapeutic equivalents — overriding the 2003 law's ban on such negotiation (section 1860D-11(i)) [S3].
Caps the plan's national monthly premium at $35 for 2006, with later years tied to the plan's actual per-capita cost including administration [S2][S3].
Lets the Secretary designate the Medicare-operated plan as the lower-premium fallback plan in regions where private plans would otherwise set the price benchmark [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers would see lower effective prices on a large volume of Medicare prescriptions, and private insurers selling Part D plans would face a competitor backed by the government's bargaining power and administrative scale [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: Setting the 2006 premium at a flat $35 nationally is a political number, not an actuarial one; if the negotiated costs plus administration exceed it, taxpayers would cover the gap, and a single national premium ignores regional cost differences [S2][S3].

A Medicare-run plan could be designated the fallback plan and would compete directly against private Part D plans, which critics argued was a step toward replacing private drug coverage with a single government plan [S3].

Savings from 'negotiation' depend entirely on how tough HHS is at the table; the bill sets no price targets or fallback authority if manufacturers refuse to deal, so the promised savings were not guaranteed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries the potential upside is concrete: a plan option with negotiated prices and a $35 entry premium. The costs fall mainly on drug makers and insurers, with some risk to taxpayers if the fixed premium underprices the plan's true cost. The bill is thin on enforcement — no price targets or penalties if manufacturers won't negotiate — so the savings were promised rather than guaranteed, but the mechanism (government bargaining, already used by the VA and other federal purchasers) is well established.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the two committees it was referred to — Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means — and its Health subcommittee, and no markup, hearing vote, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 10, 2005 by Rep. Marion Berry (D-AR) with 21 original cosponsors, the bill won 133 total cosponsors — 131 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican [S1][S4][S5].
The same day it was introduced, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, splitting jurisdiction between the two panels [S5].
On February 25, 2005 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed; no further action was recorded through the end of the 109th Congress in January 2007 [S5].

The bill targets the structure created by the 2003 Medicare drug law, which prohibited the Secretary from negotiating drug prices (section 1860D-11(i)) and routed the benefit entirely through private plans [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the ban on Medicare price negotiation and private insurers kept the Part D market to themselves; the 133-cosponsor bill died without any member having to vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private drug-plan insurers

for.name: Rep. Marion Berry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a Medicare-run drug plan with price negotiation [S1][S3][S5].

for.name: 131 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-party-of-the-minority support across the Democratic caucus [S4].

for.name: 1 House Republican and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a measure of cross-party support [S4].

against.name: Chair Joe Barton, Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Chair of a committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after its referral, leaving it in subcommittee [S5].

against.name: Chair Bill Thomas, Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Chair of a committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled action on the bill after its referral to his committee [S5].

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and PhRMA
against.what_they_did: Opposed giving the Secretary authority to negotiate Medicare drug prices, the position embodied in the 2003 law's non-negotiation clause that this bill would override.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 131 of 133 cosponsors plus the Democratic sponsor — with a single Republican and a single Independent signing on; the committees that took no action were chaired by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would require HHS to negotiate purchase prices for Medicare Part D drugs, directly reversing the statutory ban on such negotiation, which was the industry's core protection under the 2003 drug law. Lower Medicare drug prices would come largely out of manufacturers' revenues on one of their biggest customer groups [S3].

industries.industry: Private insurers and drug-plan sponsors in Medicare Part D
industries.note: Part D was built to run exclusively through private plans; a nationwide Medicare-operated plan would compete with them and could be designated the low-cost fallback plan, taking enrollment and benchmark-setting power away from private plans [S3].
